reasoning.notes: Most decisions rest on specific, checkable inference: working out types and the unowned schedule from claims and bids, reading rivals' habit of bidding above their promises, and exact payoffs for escalation and the endgame. Several pact-keeping moves in match 1 are thin, but the decisive moves rest on arithmetic that holds up.

evidence.quote: Seat 2 took round 1 (North), I am East, and round 3 went unclaimed, so South is the unowned type.
evidence.shows: Correctly works out who holds which type and which type was undealt.

evidence.quote: If seat 3 bids its agreed 2, I win at 34−4+6 = 36. Seat 1 can reach at most 34 in round 12, and seat 3 at most 33.
evidence.shows: Exact endgame calculation shows that a one-round defection secures an outright win.

evidence.quote: Raising only pays off if I'm more than 75% sure I'll be the sole raiser. Seat 2 has raised before, so I'm not that sure.
evidence.shows: Break-even odds for the escalation chicken game, combined with the rival's history.

evidence.quote: Seat 1 has bid 2 more than they promised every time so far: round 3 they said 2 and bid 4, and round 5 they said 0 and bid 6.
evidence.shows: Predicts a rival's bid from the pattern of their past lies.

evidence.quote: I lose either way. If I drop, Seat 2 wins on 11. If I raise, we both raise, and Seat 3 wins on 7.
evidence.shows: Correct case analysis of the final escalation against the totals.

planning.notes: Players openly put off defection until retaliation is no longer possible, set up rotations for the unowned rounds and carry them out over many turns, and form and break coalitions against the leader. Match 1's winner held the pact for ten rounds and then defected at the one point where no reply could catch him.

evidence.quote: any defection should come late in the game, when nobody can retaliate. For now I keep the pact.
evidence.shows: A deliberate multi-turn plan to cooperate now and defect at the end, later carried out in round 11.

evidence.quote: Both other seats said they will bid 0 and back my rotation, with me first.
evidence.shows: The rotation for unowned rounds was proposed and then followed through the game.

evidence.quote: Seat 3 may take round 10 cheaply, but I need round 12 to go uncontested, and that matters more to me.
evidence.shows: Gives up a present gain to protect a later high-value round.

evidence.quote: Seat 1 and Seat 2 may wear each other down before my 12-value round 12.
evidence.shows: Stays out so rivals spend points before its own key round.

luck.notes: Types are dealt at random but are symmetric, and the outcomes came from defections and escalation choices. Simultaneous bidding added some guesswork that moved totals at the margin.

evidence.quote: Bidding 4 should usually win this 6-value round.
evidence.shows: Blind simultaneous bids produced a three-way tie that cost everyone; the guess, not the deal, moved the totals.

weak_spots.what: Seat 3 had noted that late defection was the danger, yet bid the agreed 2 on unowned round 11 without seeing it as the leader's last safe chance to defect. A blocking bid of 4 could have forced a tie and kept the draw alive.
Seat 1 bid 6 on an unowned round worth 6, so its best case was a net 0 and a tie cost 3. It also broke its promise yet again, which isolated it. Bidding 0 was better.

Seat 1 contested the leader's high round at 6 for a best-case net of 0. This broke its word and turned both rivals against it on later rounds. A cheaper block, or a later one, would have cost less trust.

summary: Winning took real reasoning: inferring types from claims, modelling rivals' bluffs, and exact endgame and escalation arithmetic, while the decisive edge in each match came from timing a defection or a block over several turns. The game would demand more if the talk carried richer signals, or if repeated promise-breaking were costlier, so that the long run of reflexive pact-keeping turns gave way to more contested inference.
